prompt: In many large cities, ordinary working people can no longer afford to live near the places where they work. Why has this happened, and what can be done about it?
essay:
It is tempting to explain urban housing costs by pointing at somebody: foreign buyers, landlords, speculators. The difficulty with these explanations is that the same shortage appears in cities with almost no foreign investment and in cities where landlords are tightly regulated. Something more structural is at work, and it is visible in a single comparison — cities where housing is affordable are, almost without exception, cities that have recently built a great deal of it.

The binding constraint is not money or land but permission. Over the past half-century, most desirable cities have adopted rules that fix the shape of existing neighbourhoods: height limits, minimum plot sizes, requirements to preserve the character of a street. Each rule is individually reasonable and locally popular, and collectively they make it illegal to add homes in precisely the places where people most want to live. Demand then does what it must, bidding up the price of the dwellings that already exist. The people who lose are not represented in the decision, because they are the residents a city has not yet acquired.

The remedy is correspondingly unglamorous. Permitting more housing near transport, allowing existing plots to be subdivided and shortening the approval process would let supply respond to price the way it does in almost every other market. Alongside this, direct public construction is needed for the incomes that no private market will ever serve, since a builder who must recover costs cannot house a cleaner at a rent a cleaner can pay.

None of this is painless. Neighbourhoods will change, and residents who bought expecting them not to have a genuine grievance. But a city is not a museum of its own past; it is a place where people have to be able to live within reach of their work, and that requirement has to outrank a preference for an unchanged skyline.
title: When ordinary workers cannot afford the city
